title: Soulmates

jokes.text: Pawnee is the fourth most obese city in America. Soon to be number three. We're coming for you, San Antonio.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces Pawnee is the fourth most obese city in America as if it's a fact of civic life
jokes.punchline: She frames climbing to NUMBER THREE in obesity as a threat — 'We're coming for you, San Antonio' — treating this as a competitive civic achievement
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect cold-open joke because it's deeply character-specific. Only Leslie Knope would frame municipal obesity as a competitive ranking to be climbed, with civic pride. The pivot from 'we're coming for you, San Antonio' (threatening competitiveness) to 'No, we are not. We are slimming down.' is a superb self-correction that lands a second laugh. Economy is excellent — maximum information delivered fast. Justifies 8+ because the irony is layered and the character voice is unmistakable.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Pawnee is number one in obesity!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No, we are not.

jokes.text: We could have a City Hall dodgeball league! I have first pick, and my pick is Ron.
jokes.setup: Leslie is running a serious health initiative meeting, asking for ideas
jokes.punchline: Someone immediately proposes a dodgeball league and has already strategized their first pick — Ron — as if this meeting was always about dodgeball
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional laugh. The speed of the pivot to 'I have first pick, and my pick is Ron' suggests this person has been thinking about dodgeball strategy long before this meeting. Competent but not particularly inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I do a lot of cardio. I wake up at 5 AM, I run up the stairs at City Hall, I do 200 push-ups, 300 sit-ups, and a thousand yard run in below 7 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Then I take the stairs back down, and I do it all again.

jokes.text: I will be running backwards up the big hill behind the Walmart.
jokes.setup: Leslie wraps up her health initiative pitch by inviting colleagues to join her exercise routine
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'running backwards up the big hill BEHIND the Walmart' is simultaneously mundane and absurd — the Walmart geography grounds it in Pawnee's small-town reality
jokes.explanation: The joke works because of detail — it's not just a hill, it's the hill behind the Walmart, which perfectly encapsulates Pawnee's brand of provincial absurdity. Running backwards adds an extra layer of Leslie's unearned confidence in her fitness ideas.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God, did you see the way Joe was looking at Leslie? It was like he was mentally undressing her with his eyes. His pupils were dilating, his jaw was slack, he was basically drooling on himself. It was like watching a nature documentary where the male animal spots a potential mate and just completely loses all sense of decorum and self-control.

jokes.text: Don't freak out, but Joe from Sewage just unhooked your bra with his eyes.
jokes.setup: Ann warns Leslie to stay calm before delivering news
jokes.punchline: The phrasing 'unhooked your bra with his eyes' is a hyper-specific, comedically vivid way to describe being ogled — escalating a simple 'he's staring at you' to something grotesquely visual
jokes.explanation: The phrase is memorable and specific enough to be quotable. 'Don't freak out, but...' is a classic setup that primes us for something dramatic, and the payoff is absurdly specific and vivid. Strong economy — four words ('unhooked your bra with his eyes') do a lot of comedic work.

jokes.text: Van's out back. Let's roll.
jokes.setup: Joe from Sewage sidles up to Leslie and compliments her, building to a proposition
jokes.punchline: His idea of a come-on is literally inviting her to his van — the cliché of creepy van culture delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and character-specific. Joe's obliviousness to how predatory 'van's out back, let's roll' sounds is the engine of the joke. The brevity is its strength.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Red meat has been linked to heart disease, high cholesterol, and various forms of cancer.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Everything you just said is wrong. Red meat has actually made me live longer and given me the physique of a 25-year-old man.

jokes.text: If you're looking for a good time, why don't you come on down to the Toilet Party? That's what we call the Sewage Department.
jokes.setup: Joe tries to escalate his flirting by inviting Leslie somewhere
jokes.punchline: 'The Toilet Party' is the name the Sewage Department has given itself — a department nickname that inadvertently sounds like the worst possible hang
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: the Sewage Department earnestly branding themselves 'The Toilet Party' shows their blue-collar esprit de corps, and Joe presenting this as an enticement is perfect cringe comedy. 'That's what we call the Sewage Department' as the matter-of-fact explanation is the ideal deadpan tag.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Why don't you try a turkey burger? They're actually pretty good.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A turkey burger? That's just a regular burger made of turkey. I want a burger made of beef. In fact, I want two beef burgers, placed between two slices of bread that are also beef.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's just a beef sandwich.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No, it's a burger. And I'm going to have it between two pieces of bacon instead of bread.

jokes.text: Still got it, Joe. / No, you don't.
jokes.setup: Joe watches Leslie walk away and congratulates himself on his game
jokes.punchline: Ann's flat, immediate 'No, you don't' destroys his self-assessment with no elaboration
jokes.explanation: A textbook economy joke. Four words ('No, you don't.') delivered flatly is the perfect antidote to Joe's unearned swagger. The structure is clean — self-congratulation met with instant deflation. Ann as straight-woman works perfectly here.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A turkey burger? Why would anyone eat that? It's like going to a strip club and ordering a hamburger. You're there for one thing.

jokes.text: Is that a fried turkey leg inside a grilled hamburger? If so, yes. Delicious.
jokes.setup: Chris asks Ron if he's ever tried a turkey burger as a healthier alternative
jokes.punchline: Ron's definition of 'turkey burger' is a fried turkey leg inside a grilled hamburger — he has reimagined it into the most maximally meaty thing possible, then confirmed he loves it
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best character joke for Ron. It's not just a meat joke — it reveals Ron's worldview: he doesn't understand why anyone would eat anything less than maximum meat, so when presented with a 'turkey burger,' his mind naturally constructs the most indulgent interpretation. The three-beat delivery ('If so, yes. Delicious.') is perfectly economical. Only Ron Swanson could deliver this, justifying the 9.5 character integration. Comfortably in the 8+ range alongside the calibration anchors.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What do I get if I win the cook-off?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You get to watch me beat you. And then I'll beat you again. And then I'll beat you one more time, just to make sure you understand who the superior cook is.

jokes.text: Why would anyone do that to themselves?
jokes.setup: Chris explains what a turkey burger actually is — lean ground turkey formed into a patty instead of red meat
jokes.punchline: Ron's response treats eating a turkey burger as a form of self-harm or punishment
jokes.explanation: Six words that perfectly encapsulate Ron's entire food philosophy. The framing of healthy eating as self-inflicted suffering is very Ron-specific. Strong character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I got in a little trouble at the snow globe museum.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What kind of trouble?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I may have broken a snow globe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, that's not so bad. I'm completely banned from there.

jokes.text: If I win, hamburgers remain in the commissary. What do I get if I win? The rarest jewel of all. Victory over me, Ron Swanson.
jokes.setup: Ron and Chris set the stakes for their burger cook-off
jokes.punchline: Ron offers 'victory over me, Ron Swanson' as if defeating him is a prize so rare it speaks for itself — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Ron's self-regard is the joke, but it's elevated by the grandiose framing — 'the rarest jewel of all' — before the anti-climactic reveal that the jewel is just... beating Ron. His self-referential name-drop ('me, Ron Swanson') adds the perfect button. High character integration because only Ron would consider his own defeat to be a prize worth winning.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So, do you want to get dinner sometime?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I... yes, I mean... dinner is... that sounds great.

jokes.text: You know, I can't believe I'm saying this, but I actually checked out that snow globe museum that you recommended, and it was pretty awesome. Yeah. I have to say. I mean, I did get in trouble for shaking one... Yeah, I'm not allowed there anymore.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie have an enthusiastic shared-interest moment about a snow globe museum
jokes.punchline: The natural escalation leads to Ben admitting he was banned — he couldn't resist shaking the snow globes, which is both innocent and mortifying
jokes.explanation: A charming character beat that works because being banned from a snow globe museum is a very specific and gentle form of incompetence. The joke is in the escalation — from enthusiastic visitor to banned patron — and the shared understanding between Ben and Leslie before Leslie even finishes the thought.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So... babe. That's cool. We're still cool, babe.

jokes.text: Bye, babe.
jokes.setup: Ben awkwardly ends a conversation with Leslie and walks away; Tom has been observing the whole thing
jokes.punchline: Tom calls out 'Bye, babe' to Ben in a deliberately provocative way, signaling he's noticed the romantic tension and is going to make it weird
jokes.explanation: Two words that do a lot of situational work. Tom's 'babe' immediately signals he's clocked the tension and is going to weaponize it. The economy is excellent even if the joke itself isn't groundbreaking.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When I asked Ben out, he got so flustered he went to the wrong office to get his coat. He was like, 'I'll meet you at the car,' and then he walked into the Parks Department instead of going to his own office.

jokes.text: He was like, 'Huh? What? Uh... Bye.' And then he walked into an office that wasn't his.
jokes.setup: Ann asks what exactly Ben said when Leslie asked him out
jokes.punchline: Leslie's impression of Ben's flustered non-answer is funny enough, but the tag — 'he walked into an office that wasn't his' — reveals how thoroughly she rattled him
jokes.explanation: The slapstick detail of walking into the wrong office is perfectly calibrated — it's the kind of specific, embarrassing physical comedy that reveals how disoriented Ben is. Leslie's impressionistic recreation of his sputtering is charming and the tag lands clean.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Ann! No! This is... this is the worst day of my life!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I haven't even done it yet.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm just thinking about doing it.

jokes.text: Crap on a crayfish. That really stings.
jokes.setup: Ann challenges Leslie's self-pity by pointing out she's been having fun dating a bunch of guys, implying Leslie could too — and Leslie hears Ann mention she was kissing someone
jokes.punchline: Leslie's invented expletive 'Crap on a crayfish' is perfectly Pawnee — both family-friendly and oddly specific. It's followed by the reveal she was reacting to the imagined cholesterol prick, not Ann's comment
jokes.explanation: The double-layer joke works beautifully: Leslie says 'that really stings' and we think she means the emotional sting of Ann's comment, but Ann reveals she hasn't pricked her yet — Leslie was imagining the needle. 'Crap on a crayfish' is an original, quotable, character-specific expletive. High character integration because this kind of invented mild swear is quintessentially Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you are a hero. A hero!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I literally haven't done anything.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A HERO.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I haven't even taken the test yet.

jokes.text: I haven't pricked you, yet. / Oh, sorry. I was just picturing it.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'that really stings' — the audience assumes she means emotionally
jokes.punchline: Ann clarifies she hasn't pricked her yet; Leslie admits she was pre-reacting to the imagined prick
jokes.explanation: The misdirection here is clean and well-structured. The audience gets two interpretations of 'stings' and the reveal of the third one (she was imagining the prick) is a surprise that also rings true for Leslie's anxious character. The joke and its resolution are tightly paired with joke 15.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was talking to this guy named Forp.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Forp?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, Forp.

jokes.text: You're a monster.
jokes.setup: Ann suggests Leslie try Internet dating
jokes.punchline: Leslie's disproportionate response — calling Ann a monster for suggesting online dating — is funny because of the mismatch between the mild suggestion and the extreme reaction
jokes.explanation: Quick, punchy reaction. The disproportionality is the joke. Not especially original but well-delivered within the scene's rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Chris taught me all about nutrition. He said you should eat things with a lot of fiber, and things with a lot of protein, and things with a lot of vitamins.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I've been eating a bowl of fiber cereal, a bowl of protein powder, and a bowl of vitamins. All separate bowls. Sometimes I mix them together, but then it tastes like a vitamin.

jokes.text: Who the hell is Forp? / I don't know. I couldn't really hear him. It sounded like his name was Forp.
jokes.setup: Ann was apparently kissing someone outside; Leslie asks who he was
jokes.punchline: The man's name may be 'Forp' — Ann couldn't hear properly, so she's working with what she has. The name 'Forp' is inherently funny and the uncertainty makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: 'Forp' is a genuinely funny invented name because it sounds plausible enough to be real but strange enough to be absurd. The fact that Ann kissed him without knowing his name and that she's reconstructed it phonetically is efficient character comedy for both of them.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've stopped trying to understand your food choices. It's like watching someone intentionally set themselves on fire, except the fire is mozzarella sticks.

jokes.text: Get his number? / No. / Good girl.
jokes.setup: Leslie processes the 'Forp' information
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'Good girl' — delivered as if praising Ann for not getting the number of a man whose name she doesn't know — is both a mock-parental moment and a reversal of Ann's earlier role giving Leslie dating advice
jokes.explanation: Quick and efficient. Works as a comedy beat because of the reversal — the person who needs dating advice is now dispensing it. The 'Good girl' pat is brief and doesn't overstay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, Ann, how does this sound? 'I'm Leslie Knope. I love waffles, my job, and making lists. I once got drunk and told the entire Parks Department that I was in love with someone. It was the best night of my life.'

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, no. That's... why would you lead with that? Here, let me help. 'Enthusiastic public servant with a passion for her community and a quirky sense of humor. Looking for someone who can keep up with my ambition and doesn't mind if I occasionally talk about government.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, that's boring. Nobody's going to swipe right on that.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, they're not going to swipe right on yours either because you literally just described your drunk confession to the entire office.

jokes.text: Chris is a food genius. Did you know that the food you eat becomes energy? Yeah. Boom.
jokes.setup: Andy is enthusiastically overhauling the shoeshine stand with healthier snacks because of Chris's influence
jokes.punchline: Andy presents the basic fact that food becomes energy as a profound, mind-blowing revelation — 'Yeah. Boom.' — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Andy Dwyer discovering basic nutritional science as a revelation is perfect character comedy. The 'Yeah. Boom.' mic-drop delivery on information that every second-grader knows is excellently Andy-specific. High character integration — this joke only works because of who Andy is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm really into jamming.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Jamming? Like music?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, city planning. I'm jamming on zoning ordinances and municipal codes.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, 'jamming' doesn't make planning sound any cooler.

jokes.text: That's spaghetti. Nachos. That's a cookie.
jokes.setup: Andy has replaced shoeshine stand snacks with 'healthier' options; someone surveys what he's actually put out
jokes.punchline: The 'healthy' snacks Andy has selected are just regular junk food — spaghetti, nachos, a cookie — revealing Andy has no concept of nutrition despite his enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: The visual callback to Andy's 'Did you know food becomes energy?' moment is perfect. The deadpan inventory — spaghetti, nachos, cookie — delivered flatly as a series contrasting with his supposed health initiative is a strong visual gag. The escalating list structure works well.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You should take a romantic trip! Paris, Venice, the Maldives...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Those are great, but you know what's really romantic? Pawnee. Specifically the sewage treatment plant at sunset. We can get matching hard hats and really let the ambiance of industrial waste management set the mood.

jokes.text: That's my husband. See you tomorrow?
jokes.setup: Ann is at the health station; another man appears and she refers to him as her husband
jokes.punchline: The implication is Ann has been flirting with someone else (possibly in addition to Forp) and the husband's appearance is a non-surprise to her, handled with breezy calm
jokes.explanation: A brief, slightly confusing beat. Works in context as a running joke about Ann's chaotic dating life but lands softly on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why don't you just go outside and enjoy real nature?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, you know I'm terrified of bees. Out there, nature is trying to kill me. In here, the nature is fake, so it's safe. I can actually relax.

jokes.text: Yellow-haired female. Likes waffles and news. / Sexy, well-read blonde. Loves the sweeter things in life.
jokes.setup: Ann is helping Leslie write her dating profile
jokes.punchline: Leslie's unfiltered self-description ('yellow-haired female, likes waffles and news') is treated like a police report; Ann translates each phrase into normal human dating language
jokes.explanation: The contrast between Leslie's bureaucratic self-description and Ann's translation is perfectly character-specific. 'Yellow-haired female' reads like a missing persons report, while 'loves waffles' as a defining personality trait is peak Leslie. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have no opinion on turtles. I think they're just fine, but I could take them or leave them. They're fine. They're doing their thing, I'm doing mine. We're cool.

jokes.text: Organizing my agenda. / Wait, that doesn't sound fun. / Jamming on my planner.
jokes.setup: Ann asks Leslie her hobbies for the dating profile
jokes.punchline: Leslie's hobby is organizational planning, which she then reframes as 'jamming on my planner' — a phrase that tries to make bureaucracy sound edgy
jokes.explanation: 'Jamming on my planner' is a great phrase because it tries to inject Leslie's love of municipal organization with street credibility. The Ann/Leslie dynamic of Leslie describing herself robotically and Ann reframing it works very well in this sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My ideal man is mysterious, sophisticated, cultured, talented beyond measure, with a dark past that makes him complex and brooding.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's the Phantom of the Opera.

jokes.text: Favorite place? Upstairs, there is this mural of wildflowers. And I like to sit on a bench in front of it. / Really? It could be anywhere in the world. Paris, Hawaii, the Grand Canyon. / Nope. Just the bench in front of the mural.
jokes.setup: Ann asks Leslie's favorite place, implying this should be an aspirational, romantic answer
jokes.punchline: Leslie's favorite place is literally a bench in front of a mural in City Hall. She's given the chance to upgrade it and declines. Twice.
jokes.explanation: This is a great Leslie joke because it's sincere — she's not being ironic. Her favorite place in the world is a bench in City Hall, which speaks volumes about her total devotion to her job and community. The joke earns emotional resonance while being funny. When Ann escalates (Paris, Hawaii, Grand Canyon), Leslie's flat 'Nope. Just the bench in front of the mural' lands perfectly. High character integration — this only makes sense for Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm here observing. I treat healthy people like zoo animals in their natural habitat.

jokes.text: What about, like, an actual meadow where wildflowers are? / Eww, Ann. I'm scared of bees. Mural.
jokes.setup: Ann tries one more time to get Leslie to prefer an outdoor version of her mural experience
jokes.punchline: 'Eww, Ann. I'm scared of bees. Mural.' — the single-word conclusion 'Mural' as a final declaration is perfect
jokes.explanation: The callback escalation works beautifully. 'Mural.' as a one-word rebuttal and final answer is extremely quotable and perfectly encapsulates Leslie's character. The bee fear is a funny addition that justifies her indoor preference with unexpected logic. Justifies 8+ for economy and character specificity — it's a distilled character thesis in three words.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not going to make any sudden movements. These people are skittish.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: If I speak in a calm, soothing voice, I might be able to get him to eat this processed deli meat out of my hand.

jokes.text: Turtles? / No opinion. / They're condescending.
jokes.setup: Ann is running through a list of animals for the dating profile — dogs, cats, fish all get 'love' — turtles get 'no opinion'
jokes.punchline: Leslie clarifies she has no opinion on turtles because they're condescending
jokes.explanation: Three words: 'They're condescending.' This is one of the episode's best jokes. It's a pure absurdist payoff — the animal survey has built a rhythm (love, love, love) that's broken by the neutral 'no opinion,' and then the reason for no opinion is delivered with complete conviction: turtles are condescending. The specificity of the complaint (not scary, not annoying — condescending) is brilliant. Maximum economy. Easily 8+ caliber — it's the kind of specific, character-driven absurdism that makes Parks and Rec special.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Leslie! I'm so excited to hear who your match is!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, right? I've been waiting all day to tell you.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well come on, don't keep me in suspense! Who is it?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, okay... it's Ben.

jokes.text: He's dark and mysterious. And he can sing. And he plays the organ. / I think you just described the Phantom of the Opera.
jokes.setup: Ann asks Leslie to describe her ideal man
jokes.punchline: Leslie's ideal man is, piece by piece, the Phantom of the Opera — and she hadn't realized it
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured joke. The buildup ('dark and mysterious... can sing... plays the organ') escalates with each trait until Ann's recognition lands perfectly. The setup rewards attentive listening — the Phantom reveal is earned, not random. The character beat (Leslie unconsciously desiring the Phantom of the Opera) is endearing and funny simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom is like a little sister to me.

jokes.text: Leslie's reaction beat — 'Hmm.' (pause) — after being told she described the Phantom of the Opera
jokes.setup: Ann identifies that Leslie's ideal man is the Phantom of the Opera
jokes.punchline: Leslie doesn't deny it — her 'Hmm' suggests she is genuinely considering whether this is a problem
jokes.explanation: The silent beat after Ann's Phantom revelation is as important as the setup. Leslie's non-denial ('Hmm.') implies she's actually fine with this, which is funnier than a denial would be.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you met your wife on a dating site? Which one?

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Match.com

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Match.com? That's a site for people who have given up on love and are just trying to find someone, anyone, before they die alone. Your wife settled for you on a website for settlers.

jokes.text: Ah, Nirvana. Hey, guys. / Hey, Chris. / Amber. Annie. Bill. Johnny.
jokes.setup: Chris enters a health food store in Snerling and is immediately ecstatic
jokes.punchline: He greets the store as 'Nirvana' and then rattles off first names of the employees like they're old friends — suggesting he frequents this health food store 40 minutes from Pawnee regularly enough to know everyone by name
jokes.explanation: Chris's over-familiarity with a health food store in a different town is a solid character beat. The 'Nirvana' exclamation is funny given we're in an organic grocery, and the instant name-dropping of employees reveals how deeply he's integrated this 40-minute-away store into his routine.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not concerned that Andy hasn't shown up to work in three days?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ann, he does this like once a month. Last time he was missing for a week, and it turned out he was just sitting in his car in the parking lot eating pudding.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's... that's not normal behavior.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, but it's Andy behavior. There's a difference.

jokes.text: No. I don't plan to buy anything here. I buy my burger ingredients at Food and Stuff, a discount food outlet equidistant from my home and my work.
jokes.setup: Ron is inside a health food store in Snerling — seemingly the last place he'd ever be
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies he won't be buying anything; his store of choice is 'Food and Stuff,' described with the precision of a grid coordinate
jokes.explanation: 'Food and Stuff' is a perfect Ron Swanson store — maximum description with zero flair. The detail of it being 'equidistant from my home and my work' reveals Ron thinks about logistics with military precision even for grocery shopping. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You need to stop dating these guys. You have a serious problem.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. I'm going to conduct a douche-vestigation.

jokes.text: I came here for the same reason people go to the zoo.
jokes.setup: Ron explains why he came to the health food store if not to buy anything
jokes.punchline: He treats the health food store as a curiosity exhibit — exotic creatures to observe, not interact with
jokes.explanation: This is one of Ron's best one-liners. The zoo analogy perfectly frames his relationship with health food culture — not disgusted, not angry, just fascinated by it as a foreign ecosystem. The economy is exceptional. Justifies 8+ because the zoo metaphor is genuinely original and the delivery elevates it further. It also sets up the visual gag that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What do you look for in women?

dialogue.speaker: Joe
dialogue.line: Pulse. Optional.

jokes.text: Shh. Look at that thing. [Ron observing an exotic health food item on the shelf]
jokes.setup: Ron has compared himself to a zoo visitor; he now actually behaves like one
jokes.punchline: Ron 'shushes' someone (presumably Chris or April) and whispers 'Look at that thing,' pointing at a health food product as if it were a rare animal
jokes.explanation: The physical payoff of joke 32. Ron immediately acting out the zoo metaphor — shushing people, whispering, pointing at a health food item in genuine fascination — is perfect visual execution of the setup. The callback elevates both jokes. Justifies 8+ because the commitment to the bit and the visual execution are exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Store employee
dialogue.line: We have a vegan bacon option.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm intrigued.

jokes.text: Nature is amazing.
jokes.setup: Ron has been treating health food like zoo animals
jokes.punchline: He concludes his observation with 'Nature is amazing' — treating a health food product as a wildlife encounter
jokes.explanation: The button on the zoo sequence. 'Nature is amazing' works as Ron's sincere appreciation for the absurd health food item, completing the trifecta of zoo jokes. Three words, maximum impact, perfect character voice. The economy alone (9.5) elevates this.

dialogue.speaker: Store employee
dialogue.line: Sir, you can't eat all the samples.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm doing this for everyone's safety. Someone needs to make sure these vegan products are actually inedible.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, I actually wanted to try one.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Too late. I've neutralized the threat.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. A 98% match? That's a soul mate-level match. I've never seen anything this high before.
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie are excitedly reviewing the dating site matches
jokes.punchline: Ann has found a 98% soul mate match for Leslie, establishing high stakes for who this perfect person might be — creating anticipation before the eventual reveal that it's Tom
jokes.explanation: Primarily a setup moment rather than a punchline, but it functions as part of the Tom-reveal joke structure. On its own it's functional setup comedy. Earns rewatch bonus because knowing it's Tom makes Ann's breathless '98%' funnier.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm eating healthy now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well I made something called 'Andy's Mouth Surprise.'

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's a terrible name for an already terrible food.

jokes.text: This is Craig at hoosiermate.com. How can I help you? / Craig, your service is crap. / Can you be more specific?
jokes.setup: Leslie calls the dating site's customer service to complain about her match
jokes.punchline: Her opening complaint is simply 'your service is crap' — blunt to the point of being unprofessional — and Craig's calm 'Can you be more specific?' treats this as a normal service call
jokes.explanation: The subversion of expected phone complaint etiquette — Leslie skips pleasantries entirely — is good character comedy. Craig's professional patience against Leslie's bluntness is a nice contrast.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have names for all my foods. Breakfast food is 'morning magic.' Lunch is 'noon noms.' Dinner is 'evening feast.' Snacks between meals are 'flavor soldiers.' Dessert is 'sweet dream team.' Beverages are 'liquid joy.' Condiments are 'flavor ninjas.' Cheese is 'dairy gold.' Bacon is 'meat candy.' And pizza is just 'pizza' because pizza is perfect and needs no improvement.

jokes.text: I actually met my wife on the site. / Really? / Well, that's not gonna last. / Excuse me? / You heard me. Your marriage is a sham. Goodbye, Craig.
jokes.setup: Craig defends his site's algorithm by mentioning it worked for him personally — he met his wife on it
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately diagnoses his marriage as doomed and declares it a sham, then hangs up
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best moments. The escalation from complaint call to 'your marriage is a sham' is unexpected and perfectly Leslie — she's furious about the algorithm and the collateral damage is Craig's marriage. 'You heard me' as a bridge to 'Goodbye, Craig' is excellent structure. Justifies 8+ because the escalation is genuinely surprising and the delivery ('Your marriage is a sham. Goodbye, Craig.') is impeccably constructed for maximum comedic impact.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: If you had three wishes, what would they be?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: First wish: a lifetime supply of Sweetums candy and soda, but only the limited edition flavors.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Second wish: a 2015 Lexus, fully loaded.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Third wish: more wishes.

jokes.text: He seems nice. / Eh, he kind of lives in a barn.
jokes.setup: Ann observes after the Craig call that he seemed like a reasonable person
jokes.punchline: Leslie dismisses him with 'he kind of lives in a barn' — used casually as a disqualifying character trait delivered as throwaway information
jokes.explanation: Efficient and funny. The casual delivery of 'he kind of lives in a barn' as a reason to dismiss someone implies Leslie has more information about Craig than she should. The 'eh' opener makes the dismissal even more casual.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, I wish that Jamie Foxx and I become best friends. We hang out all the time. We go to Lakers games together. We get matching tattoos. His says 'Tom' and mine says 'Jamie.' But then one day he's like, 'Hey man, I'm going to Africa to build schools.' And I'm like, 'I'm coming with you, brother!' So we go to Africa and we're building schools, but then I realize I'm better at it than him. So I start building schools without him. And pretty soon I'm like the most famous school builder in the world. And Jamie Foxx calls me crying like, 'Why did you leave me?' And I'm like, 'Because I'm better than you, Jamie.'

jokes.text: But for whatever reason, right now, only douchey guys are buying what you're selling.
jokes.setup: Ann is giving Leslie a pep talk but needs to be honest about the current situation
jokes.punchline: The clinical/commercial framing — 'buying what you're selling' — applied to romantic attraction is an unusual but precise metaphor that lands funny
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat that sets up the 'douche-vestigation' joke. The marketplace metaphor is mildly funny but not exceptionally crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: He wants to play both leads in a Point Break remake

jokes.text: So, I should go and ask them what they think I'm selling. / A douche-vestigation. / Nice.
jokes.setup: Leslie decides to interrogate the gross men who are attracted to her
jokes.punchline: Ann coins 'douche-vestigation' and Leslie immediately validates it with 'Nice.'
jokes.explanation: 'Douche-vestigation' is a genuinely good portmanteau — specific, funny, and immediately understood. Leslie's instant 'Nice.' approval is the perfect button. High quotability because it's the kind of word that sticks. The structure (Leslie states the plan, Ann names it, Leslie approves) is efficient and satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, can you grab me some milk, eggs, and bread?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Sure. Also, I named the shopping cart Mittens.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why Mittens?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I named the other one Professor Whiskers and the third one is just called Steven.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What's the logic?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: There is none. I just do things.

jokes.text: I know you're gonna take this the wrong way, but can I talk to you for a second? / You can do anything to me, for any number of seconds.
jokes.setup: Leslie approaches Joe to ask about his attraction to her, preemptively warning him not to misread it
jokes.punchline: Joe completely misreads it anyway, immediately — 'You can do anything to me, for any number of seconds' is both creepy and oddly poetic
jokes.explanation: Joe's response is funny because it's oddly formal and all-encompassing in its creepiness — 'for any number of seconds' adds a bureaucratic precision to what should be a simple leer. The callback to Leslie's warning ('I know you're gonna take this the wrong way') being immediately proven correct is excellent structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, I just want to share some of my accomplishments with you. In high school, I was voted most likely to succeed, I was captain of the debate team, and I had a brief lesbian experience.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Go back to the lesbian thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It was just experimental, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't care, keep going.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I also graduated summa cum laude and I've been published in three academic journals.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay, I'm gonna go.

jokes.text: She can't be in a wheelchair. No canes. No gray hair.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Joe what he looks for in a woman, hoping to understand why he's attracted to her
jokes.punchline: Joe's checklist for a potential partner is entirely about ruling out the elderly and disabled — his standards are exclusively 'not old or infirm'
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Joe's standards are comically low — his entire filter is 'ambulatory and not elderly.' The list structure (wheelchair, canes, gray hair) builds to a funny specificity. Leslie's realization — 'So you're basically attracted to me because I'm not an elderly person' — is the even better payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I go to a store called 'The Container Store.' I love it. I'm very literal. So I assumed it was a store that sells containers. It is. But I also assumed that, eventually, they would just be selling the store itself in a container. Like, a little tiny store, that fits in a container. I'm still waiting.

jokes.text: So, basically, you're just attracted to me because I'm not an elderly person.
jokes.setup: Joe has listed his requirements: no wheelchairs, no canes, no gray hair
jokes.punchline: Leslie's blunt summary of his criteria — passing the bar of 'not elderly' — is deflating and perfectly delivered
jokes.explanation: The perfect summation of Joe's requirements. Leslie articulating her own appeal as simply 'not being elderly' is a brilliant deflation of her earlier insecurity about why Joe was attracted to her. The callback structure is tight and the payoff is earned.

dialogue.speaker: Cashier
dialogue.line: Will that be all for you today?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes. I have everything I need: bacon, eggs, and Scotch. A man could live on these three things alone.

dialogue.speaker: Cashier
dialogue.line: That's... quite a diet.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's not a diet. It's a way of life.

jokes.text: Yeah. And as I aforementioned, you have a killer dumpster.
jokes.setup: Joe confirms Leslie's assessment and adds one more positive quality
jokes.punchline: 'Killer dumpster' — Joe's compliment is Sewage Department slang for posterior, but he has also literally said 'aforementioned' in a sentence, which reveals he's more articulate than expected in the worst possible moment
jokes.explanation: The word 'aforementioned' doing heavy lifting here makes the joke exceptional. Joe is a sewage worker who leers at women, but he uses 'aforementioned' correctly in a sentence — the vocabulary sophistication in service of a vulgar compliment is a perfect incongruity. 'Killer dumpster' as sewage-worker slang is inspired. This comfortably justifies 8+ because the incongruity of 'aforementioned' and 'killer dumpster' in the same breath is genuinely original and specifically character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, you got a match on the dating site!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, did you set this up? Did you create a fake profile to match with me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No! It's a real person.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So you're telling me an actual human woman swiped right on me? That seems... unlikely.

jokes.text: Leslie's reaction to 'killer dumpster' — a stunned silent beat before the scene cuts
jokes.setup: Joe delivers 'killer dumpster' as a compliment
jokes.punchline: Leslie's silence — the complete absence of a response — is funnier than anything she could say
jokes.explanation: The silent beat after 'killer dumpster' is the appropriate response. In a mockumentary format, this likely includes a camera look. The absence of words is the correct comedic choice and shows good structural instincts.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo. Leslie and me, we got something special. It's like... *beatboxing* Leslie in the place to be, Tom Haverford, that's me. We're dating now, yeah. Her love is like a government contract, I don't understand it but I'm gonna profit off it. Boom!

jokes.text: Would you like to sample our vegan bacon? 100% meatless. / Yes, please.
jokes.setup: An employee at the health food store offers Ron a sample of vegan bacon
jokes.punchline: Ron, who has treated the entire health food store as a zoo exhibit, says 'Yes, please' with apparent sincerity — showing his curiosity overrides his ideology when meat-adjacent products are involved
jokes.explanation: The setup is Ron as zoo visitor, so him accepting vegan bacon is slightly against expectation. But the real punch comes in what follows — the tasting reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This place has great bones. Perfect for a young family. We could put the nursery right there, convert the garage into a man cave for me... Obviously, I'd need to negotiate that with my future wife.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm thinking we get married in the spring, honeymoon in Bora Bora, have our first kid by next year. It's all very doable if we play our cards right.

jokes.text: Sir? Is there a problem? / I'm just making sure no one ever has to eat this. / I don't think I can give you any more.
jokes.setup: Ron has been eating all the vegan bacon samples; an employee intervenes
jokes.punchline: Ron's stated reason for consuming all samples is to prevent anyone else from eating them — an act of sabotage framed as public service
jokes.explanation: 'I'm just making sure no one ever has to eat this.' Justifies 8+ comfortably. The logic is pure Ron: he disagrees with vegan bacon on principle and has therefore appointed himself its executioner, framing destruction as a public service. The statement has perfect deadpan structure, is deeply character-specific, and is immediately quotable. This is one of Ron Swanson's all-time great lines.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm really uncomfortable right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's what I'm here for. I'm like a human blanket, but instead of warmth, I provide crippling anxiety and a strong smell of cologne.

jokes.text: Yeah, I'm calling to lodge a complaint about the seaweed and almond under-eye cream I purchased from you guys. My problem is it smells terrible. Yeah, I even mixed it with another under-eye cream and it still smelled. So, I ruined two eye creams. Yes, I will hold.
jokes.setup: While Ron and Chris are busy in the health food store, April is on her phone making a complaint call
jokes.punchline: April — who affects total apathy about everything — is deeply invested in the quality of her seaweed and almond under-eye cream. The complaint escalates when she reveals she tried to fix the cream by mixing it with another eye cream and 'ruined two eye creams'
jokes.explanation: The surprise of April caring deeply about eye cream (vs. her affect of not caring about anything) is excellent character subversion. 'I ruined two eye creams' as an escalating self-own is funny because April narrates her own incompetence with complete investment. The 'Yes, I will hold' button shows she's committed to this cause. High character integration because it plays against April's usual persona.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So... this is awkward.

jokes.text: [April singing 'Forever Young' while on hold during the eye cream complaint call]
jokes.setup: April is on hold after her eye cream complaint
jokes.punchline: She absentmindedly sings along to the hold music — 'Forever Young' — which is thematically ironic given the anti-aging eye cream context
jokes.explanation: The irony of anti-aging cream + 'Forever Young' hold music is a nice passive joke. April singing along unselfconsciously is a good character beat — she's too committed to the complaint to notice the irony.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need to get our heart rates up.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's what she said.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Tom!

jokes.text: What's this? / Dragon fruit. / What's this? / A kiwano, or horned melon. / What's this? / A peach. / I knew that.
jokes.setup: Andy is asking Chris to identify exotic fruits in the health food store
jokes.punchline: The first two items are legitimately exotic (dragon fruit, kiwano). The third is a peach. Andy's 'I knew that' is a defensive save that reveals he didn't know it
jokes.explanation: The structure here is impeccable. Two legitimately exotic items lull the audience into thinking this is an education montage, then the punchline is 'a peach' — the most common fruit possible — followed by Andy's preemptive defensive 'I knew that' which confirms he absolutely did not know it. Perfect escalation/deflation structure. Justifies 8+ for structural execution.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, Leslie, I'm gonna be a millionaire by next year. I can feel it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, you'd be lucky if you had a million dollars by next lifetime.

jokes.text: What's your favorite food? / Well, I take Skittles, and I put it between two Starbursts. / Skittle sandwich? / That's pretty good. / No, I call it Andy's mouth surprise.
jokes.setup: Chris asks Andy his favorite food, presumably expecting something earnest in the health food context
jokes.punchline: Andy has invented a candy construction — Skittles between Starbursts — and named it 'Andy's mouth surprise.' He also rejects the more intuitive 'Skittle sandwich' name, which he compliments
jokes.explanation: 'Andy's mouth surprise' is an excellent Andy Dwyer invention — the proprietary name for a candy sandwich he invented implies the existence of an entire Andy Dwyer culinary catalog. His gracious acknowledgment of 'Skittle sandwich' as 'pretty good' before correcting it to his inferior-named version is perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I walked into a glass door at the Apple Store. It's not a problem though, because I'm covered by AppleCare.

jokes.text: It's nice because the flavor of the Starbursts really bring out a similar flavor in the Skittles.
jokes.setup: Andy explains the gastronomic logic behind Andy's mouth surprise
jokes.punchline: His flavor pairing rationale — 'the Starbursts really bring out a similar flavor in the Skittles' — sounds like food criticism but describes combining two candy brands that are basically the same thing
jokes.explanation: Andy applying the language of sommelier/chef pairing ('bring out a similar flavor') to explain why two fruit-flavored candies taste good together is great character comedy. The absurd logic is delivered with complete earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Mmm, this is delicious! What is this?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's the garnish.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Do you wanna go to lunch? / No, I don't really feel like going to J.J.'s. / We can go anywhere. Your choice. I'm buying. / Can I get apps and 'zerts?
jokes.setup: Tom asks Leslie to lunch; she initially declines
jokes.punchline: When Tom says she can pick anywhere and he's buying, Leslie's first move is to negotiate — immediately asking if she can get appetizers and desserts, nicknamed 'apps' and ''zerts'
jokes.explanation: The abbreviation ''zerts' for desserts is a preview of the full Tom vocabulary bit to follow. Leslie's food-forward negotiation is good character work but the setup for a bigger joke.

jokes.text: 'Zerts are what I call desserts. Tray-trays are entrees. I call sandwiches sammies, sandoozles, or Adam Sandlers. Air conditioners are cool blasterz, with a Z. I don't know where that came from. I call cakes big ol' cookies. I call noodles long-ass rice. Fried chicken is fry-fry chicky-chick. Chicken parm is chicky-chicky parm-parm. Chicken cacciatore? Chicky catch. I call eggs pre-birds or future birds. Root beer is super water. Tortillas are bean blankies. And I call forks food rakes.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks about Tom's abbreviation ''zerts' for desserts
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals an entire private vocabulary for food items, each nickname more absurd than the last — building from mildly reasonable (sammies) to completely unhinged (pre-birds or future birds for eggs, food rakes for forks)
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's standout joke and one of Parks and Recreation's all-time great bits. The escalation is masterfully constructed: it starts with reasonable abbreviations ('sammies'), accelerates through oddly specific alternatives ('sandoozles, or Adam Sandlers'), and then goes fully unhinged ('long-ass rice' for noodles, 'pre-birds or future birds' for eggs, 'food rakes' for forks). Each new item lands bigger than the last. The self-deprecating aside ('I don't know where that came from' for cool blasterz) breaks the fourth wall perfectly. 'Food rakes' as the final button may be the best single item. This is a cultural touchstone moment for the show — easily calibrated against the 9.5 anchor. Justifies 9+ across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not gonna lie to you. Leslie is a really good kisser.

jokes.text: You can get as many 'zerts as you want. / Well, let's get in my go-go mobile. / Car.
jokes.setup: Leslie agrees to lunch after the vocabulary list; Tom continues his naming scheme
jokes.punchline: 'Go-go mobile' for car — Leslie's flat 'Car.' correction is the perfect foil to Tom's enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: The callback to Tom's vocabulary list lands perfectly. Leslie's single-word correction 'Car.' is the ideal straight-man response — minimal, dismissive, and funny. The escalation continues from the list and her refusal to engage with it is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: This tastes like I'm eating Beyoncé's hair.

jokes.text: I have a huge house with a ton of balconies. And I would just stand out there and survey my empire, like a drug dealer in a Michael Bay movie. And I'll just spend my time out there reading my iPad and drinking espressos in a terry cloth robe.
jokes.setup: Tom's first genie wish
jokes.punchline: The specificity of the wish escalates from (house with balconies) to (surveying empire like a drug dealer in a Michael Bay movie) to (iPad + espressos + terry cloth robe) — each detail more specific and revealing of Tom's self-image
jokes.explanation: The dream is character-perfect. 'Like a drug dealer in a Michael Bay movie' is a specific, original reference that perfectly encapsulates Tom's aspirational self-image — he wants to feel powerful but in an extremely specific cinematic way. The terry cloth robe + espresso + iPad addition shows his luxury is defined by very specific objects. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Kyle
dialogue.line: Saffron and umami are really essential to this dish.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh come on, dude. You're being so pretentious right now.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, that was rude. You're right, saffron is great.

jokes.text: I'm the CEO of the Spike TV network. And my best friend slash personal assistant is Oscar winner Jamie Foxx. And we create a raunchy animated series based on our friendship, called Tommy and the Foxx.
jokes.setup: Tom's second genie wish
jokes.punchline: The wish is a complete career/lifestyle fantasy — CEO of Spike TV, best friends with Jamie Foxx, animated series — 'Tommy and the Foxx' as the title is perfect Tom Haverford branding
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Tom's wishes is what makes them exceptional. He doesn't want generic fame — he wants to run Spike TV specifically, be best friends with Jamie Foxx specifically, and have an animated show with a punny title. 'Tommy and the Foxx' is brilliant because it's exactly the kind of title Tom Haverford would choose for his vanity project. Justifies 8+ because the specificity transcends generic 'I want to be famous' and becomes a precise portrait of Tom's self-mythology.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'll have a burger. A meat sandwich. Between two pieces of bread.

jokes.text: They remake Point Break. I play both roles. Keanu and Swayze.
jokes.setup: Tom's third and final genie wish
jokes.punchline: After two elaborate wishes, his final wish is to play both Keanu Reeves AND Patrick Swayze in a Point Break remake — no context, no explanation, just total commitment
jokes.explanation: The best of the three wishes and a standalone classic line. The structure is perfect: the first two wishes were elaborate and specific, then the third is delivered in three short sentences — 'They remake Point Break. I play both roles. Keanu and Swayze.' The economy is exceptional (9.5). The desire to play both roles is brilliantly insane and the specification of 'Keanu and Swayze' (as if the listener might not know who's in Point Break) is the perfect button. This comfortably justifies 8+ and approaches the 'snip snap' calibration level for pure character absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, why did my burger lose? I don't understand.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Oh. I guess I haven't eaten my competition in years.

jokes.text: I think if you continue cross-training the way you have, you're gonna... [Chris sees Ron hasn't bought any ingredients] I don't see any ingredients. Have you bought ingredients? / Nope.
jokes.setup: Chris has been enthusiastically coaching Ron through the health food store in preparation for the burger cook-off
jokes.punchline: Ron hasn't bought a single thing despite being in the store — his 'Nope' is delivered with the complete calm of a man who never had any intention of buying anything
jokes.explanation: A payoff on Ron's earlier announcement that he wasn't there to buy anything. The 'Nope' is perfectly Ron — no explanation, no apology, complete serenity. Callbacks to his stated position from the beginning of the store visit.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I swear on this dead crow, I will win that burger contest.

jokes.text: Chris! Can I get these? [Andy appears at checkout with a comically random selection of items]
jokes.setup: Ron has bought nothing; the camera cuts to Andy who has somehow found items to purchase
jokes.punchline: Andy's selections in a health food store are presumably as random and non-healthy as his earlier snack choices at the shoeshine stand
jokes.explanation: Quick beat. Works as a callback to Andy's nutritional confusion. Limited without seeing what he's actually holding.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I have a strict no-dating policy in the workplace. It's a distraction, it compromises judgment, and it creates an uncomfortable dynamic that affects the entire department.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's a really good policy, actually.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, Chris, that makes total sense.

jokes.text: Honey? / Pinwheel.
jokes.setup: Chris responds to Andy asking about items — the transcript implies a confusing brief exchange
jokes.punchline: Chris calls something a 'pinwheel' in response to Andy's 'Honey?' — suggesting Andy found something he thought was honey but Chris identifies as a pinwheel, or this is Chris's nickname for something
jokes.explanation: Unclear from transcript alone — this may be a visual gag that reads better on screen. Scored conservatively.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you won't believe what happened. I just found out I'm allergic to something.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? To what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the thing — the doctor doesn't even know. He said it could be the beef, the bun, the condiments, or some mysterious ingredient he's never seen before.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So you don't know what to avoid?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Nope. I'm basically allergic to mystery now.

jokes.text: I love sunshine and fresh air and early-morning walks. / One. / I've read five biographies of Eleanor Roosevelt. / One. / I work at the Parks and Recreation... / One. / That's what you do. / One.
jokes.setup: Tom plays a game where Leslie rates his statements on a scale of 1-10 in terms of interest; he's ostensibly probing what she finds attractive
jokes.punchline: Every single thing Leslie mentions about herself — sunshine, Eleanor Roosevelt, her job — gets rated a '1' by Tom, who is rating her attributes by his own shallow standards
jokes.explanation: The escalating string of '1's is well-executed. Tom's complete indifference to everything Leslie values is character comedy gold — his shallow worldview rendering her earnest self-description completely unappealing to him. The rhythm of setup-one, setup-one, setup-one builds effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Online dating is like a game show where you have to pick a door, except all the doors are broken and one of them has a guy named Derek inside.

jokes.text: I once kissed a girl in college. / Eight.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been getting '1' for everything she says; she throws in this detail presumably to test him
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately jumps from '1' to '8' — his interest is entirely driven by that specific detail
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the rating game. The jump from 1 to 8 in response to that specific detail is the expected subversion but delivered with good timing. The follow-up where Tom's interest collapses back to zero with additional information is the second laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've decided to just accept things as they are. No more fighting City Hall. I'm going to embrace the status quo.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, really? That doesn't sound like you at all.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm serious. I'm going to date you and just... settle.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes! Finally!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just kidding. I would never.

jokes.text: I love Food and Stuff. It's where I buy all of my food. And most of my stuff.
jokes.setup: Ron unprompted endorses his preferred grocery store
jokes.punchline: The tautological description — 'I buy all of my food. And most of my stuff.' — perfectly captures Ron's relationship with a discount grocery store called Food and Stuff
jokes.explanation: The logic of 'Food and Stuff' as a store name contains its own punchline — the store is called what it sells. Ron completing the tautology with 'And most of my stuff' implies he also buys his non-food possessions there, which is the exact kind of efficient, practical Ron behavior that makes him funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I have like five different dating profiles. I got my main one, my backup, my nerd one that I never check...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you matched with your nerd profile?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the one you never check?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Hey, can I get these? / How much are they? / Two bucks apiece. / Good deal. / Anything else? / Nope. Just the crows and the beef.
jokes.setup: Ron shops at Food and Stuff, asking about prices in his usual no-nonsense way
jokes.punchline: 'Just the crows and the beef' — Ron is buying dead crows alongside his burger meat as a completely ordinary shopping transaction
jokes.explanation: The deadpan reveal that Ron is purchasing crows alongside his beef — in the same transaction, with no explanation — is a brilliant absurdist Ron moment. The casual 'just the crows and the beef' implies the crows are the mundane part of the purchase. This is deeply Ron-specific and highly quotable. Justifies 8+ because the absurdism is earned through complete deadpan delivery — Ron doesn't explain the crows, which is funnier than any explanation could be.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My favorite movie is books.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, that's not even... books aren't movies.

jokes.text: So, the only thing that's important to you is hotness? Wendy? Lucy? All you cared about was the shape of their boobs? / No, I really liked them, and they happened to have nice breasts.
jokes.setup: Leslie interrogates Tom about his past relationships in the context of the douche-vestigation
jokes.punchline: Tom's defense — 'I really liked them, and they happened to have nice breasts' — is almost gallant in its framing, as if he's clearing up an unfair characterization
jokes.explanation: Tom's defense is character-appropriate and mildly funny. The framing of physical attraction as incidental ('they happened to have') is a classic male-comedy deflection. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: If you ever talk about your dating profiles again, I will kill you in your sleep.

jokes.text: You're acting really weird. What did you even buy me lunch for? Just so you could yell at me for what I like about women?
jokes.setup: Leslie has been aggressively questioning Tom about his shallow taste
jokes.punchline: Tom's complaint that he's being interrogated about his preferences at a lunch he paid for is technically valid — he has a point that this is a terrible date
jokes.explanation: A functional complaint beat. Works as a reality check on how weird the 'date' has gotten but not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: This is insane, but you and I got matched up on hoosiermate.com. 98% match. Soul mate-level match. / You wanna date me! This is a date! / This is not a date, okay? You took me to a fancy restaurant, you paid for my meal, and you're trying to get to know me better.
jokes.setup: Leslie reveals the 98% match to Tom
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately and correctly points out that by all objective criteria, this IS a date. Leslie's denial crumbles against his point-by-point analysis of what constitutes a date
jokes.explanation: Tom's legal-style argument that this is definitionally a date is good comedic structure. His checklist (fancy restaurant, paid for meal, trying to get to know me better) against Leslie's 'this is not a date' denial is a classic misdirection payoff. The reveal works well in the episode context.

jokes.text: [Tom begins singing a rap/song about Leslie and Tom dating as they leave the restaurant]
jokes.setup: Tom has declared this a date; Leslie is mortified
jokes.punchline: Tom performs an improvised song — 'Leslie Knope, Tom Haverford / Dating in the day, dating in the night...' — in public, completely unselfconscious
jokes.explanation: Tom composing and performing a spontaneous rap about his and Leslie's relationship while walking out of a restaurant is deeply Tom Haverford. The lines are intentionally bad ('dating on the floor / cause she wants some more') which is part of the joke — Tom thinks this is great. Highly character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh, this is perfect for us. Three-bedroom, and... Oh, God, Les. It has that dream closet you've always wanted. A walk-in closet. Oh, God. Hey, hey, boo. What's wrong? Where did you go? Come back to me. / Stop it. / Don't disappear on me. I need you, boo.
jokes.setup: Tom is at a computer looking at real estate while also printing health tips for Leslie
jokes.punchline: Tom has become so committed to the 'they're dating' bit that he's now browsing three-bedroom apartments and calling Leslie 'boo' with performative romantic distress
jokes.explanation: Tom's escalation of the dating bit from a song to apartment-hunting is excellent escalation comedy. 'Come back to me, boo' and 'Don't disappear on me' delivered with soap-opera intensity about a three-bedroom apartment listing is peak Tom Haverford. The specificity of 'a walk-in closet you've always wanted' shows Tom has done research on Leslie's preferences.

jokes.text: Ben, if it's okay with you, Leslie and I are going to lead the meeting today, because of our deep spiritual connection.
jokes.setup: Tom and Leslie arrive at a work meeting
jokes.punchline: Tom announces to Ben (their supervisor/colleague) that he and Leslie will be leading the meeting due to their 'deep spiritual connection' — bringing the fake-dating bit into a professional context
jokes.explanation: Tom refusing to break character in a professional setting is good sustained comedy. 'Deep spiritual connection' as a reason to lead a work meeting is funny because it's both absurd and entirely in character for how Tom conducts himself.

jokes.text: There is some weird juju in this room right now.
jokes.setup: Ben is clearly uncomfortable with Tom's behavior at the meeting
jokes.punchline: Tom narrates the awkward atmosphere he created as external phenomenon — 'weird juju' — rather than acknowledging it's his behavior causing it
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat. Tom's obliviousness to being the source of the weirdness is character-appropriate but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: We give everyone pedometers and we have a contest. Whoever takes the most steps wins a prize. Anything to get their heart rate up. / You know what else gets people's heart rate up? / Doing it. / Talking about sex with my boss.
jokes.setup: Leslie presents pedometer contest as a health initiative idea
jokes.punchline: Tom's 'Doing it' as a heart-rate elevator — and his immediate talking-head confession 'Talking about sex with my boss' — makes the inappropriateness of the comment the joke itself
jokes.explanation: The 'Doing it' joke itself is a bit predictable, but the talking-head confession — 'Talking about sex with my boss' — reframes it by showing Tom is aware of the line he's crossing and has chosen to cross it anyway. The self-awareness elevates it slightly above the baseline dirty joke.

jokes.text: What is wrong with you? Leslie. It's the workplace. You're being a little bit too feisty right now. / You are being a little bit too much of an ass right now. Okay? Knock it off.
jokes.setup: Leslie pulls Tom out of the meeting to confront him
jokes.punchline: Tom's accusation that she's being 'feisty' in the workplace — as if his sexual innuendo was appropriate but her reaction isn't — is perfectly oblivious. Leslie's flat 'you are being a little bit too much of an ass right now' matches his phrasing in a satisfying mirror
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure — Tom accuses her of being 'a little bit too feisty,' she counters 'a little bit too much of an ass' — is satisfying mirror comedy. Tom's reversal of responsibility is character-perfect.

jokes.text: I can't fight this feeling anymore. You and I, we're dating. / You should be so lucky.
jokes.setup: Tom doubles down on the dating declaration
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'You should be so lucky' — dismissive but delivered with a trace of real annoyance — is perfect. It's almost complimentary to herself while shutting him down
jokes.explanation: Quick and punchy. 'You should be so lucky' is a solid put-down that works because it's confident rather than defensive.

jokes.text: It was all just a joke. I can assure you, there's nothing romantic going on between me and Tom. I have a very strict policy. No office relationships, particularly between a supervisor and an employee.
jokes.setup: Leslie addresses the camera in a talking head after the Tom incident
jokes.punchline: Leslie's very serious declaration of her anti-office-romance policy, delivered with extreme formality, is ironic because we know she's actively pining for Ben — her boss/supervisor figure — and the Ben relationship is where this episode is clearly heading
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony is the engine of this joke. Leslie's emphatic statement of 'no office relationships' while being in the middle of developing feelings for Ben (who also works in the office) is satisfying situational irony. Earns rewatch bonus because it's funnier knowing the arc of the season.

jokes.text: Look. Cucumber flower. / Wow, that's so cute. / Wait, that's a garnish. You're not supposed to eat that. / What?
jokes.setup: Chris and Leslie are at lunch; Chris points out something decorative on the plate
jokes.punchline: Leslie has apparently already eaten it — her 'What?' in response to being told it's decorative suggests she had no idea and has been cheerfully eating garnishes
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional food comedy beat. Leslie eating a garnish and being baffled that it wasn't edible is a small character moment — her guilelessness around food rules.

jokes.text: Fine. We got matched up on an online dating site. And I was messing with her, she got pissed. So, she took me out in the hallway and kissed me, out of revenge. / Really? / And as much as it pains me to admit this, it was not disgusting. / Okay. Well, I don't need the details. / I'm just saying. She knows what to do. / Like, I was impressed. / Yeah. / It was stirring. / Goodbye. / It felt like...
jokes.setup: Ben asks Tom what happened with Leslie; Tom explains the dating site match and the revenge kiss
jokes.punchline: Tom's review of the kiss escalates from 'not disgusting' (a low bar) to 'she knows what to do' to 'I was impressed' to 'stirring' — each descriptor more poetic and inappropriate, while Ben tries increasingly hard to shut down the conversation
jokes.explanation: This scene is exceptional because of the escalating descriptor chain for the kiss. Starting at 'not disgusting' (a backhanded non-compliment), climbing through 'she knows what to do,' 'I was impressed,' to 'stirring' — and then the cut-off 'It felt like...' implying there's even more — is brilliant escalation structure. Tom becoming unexpectedly sincere about how good the kiss was while Ben desperately tries to end the conversation adds dramatic irony (Ben has feelings for Leslie). 'It was stirring' is probably the peak quotable word — an unexpected adjective that sounds both sincere and slightly romantic from Tom. Justifies 8+ for structure, character integration, and impact.

jokes.text: I humbly place before you my east-meets-west patented Traeger Turkey Burger, an Asian-fusion burger made with Willow Farms organic turkey, a toasted taleggio cheese crisp, papaya chutney, black truffle aioli, and microgreens on a gluten-free brioche bun. Enjoy.
jokes.setup: The burger cook-off begins; Chris presents his entry
jokes.punchline: Chris's presentation is a parody of pretentious food culture — 'east-meets-west patented,' 'Willow Farms organic,' 'taleggio cheese crisp,' 'truffle aioli,' 'microgreens,' 'gluten-free brioche' — it's the complete checklist of food-trend buzzwords circa 2010
jokes.explanation: Chris's burger presentation is a food-culture satire that works because every element is recognizably try-hard. The 'east-meets-west patented' is the funniest element — the idea that Chris has trademarked his fusion approach. Good character integration.

jokes.text: This tastes as delicious as Beyoncé smells. I'm guessing.
jokes.setup: Someone tastes Chris's burger and wants to compliment it
jokes.punchline: 'As delicious as Beyoncé smells. I'm guessing.' — the Beyoncé comparison is an unusual and vivid simile for taste, with 'I'm guessing' acknowledging that this is speculation about a stranger's scent
jokes.explanation: The simile is genuinely original — tasting like a celebrity smells is an unusual cross-sensory compliment. The 'I'm guessing' tag is essential because it acknowledges the speaker hasn't actually smelled Beyoncé, which makes the whole thing funnier rather than undermining it. High originality and quotability. A strong 8+ candidate.

jokes.text: What is this in here? Saffron? / Wow! Somebody's got a sharp palate. / I love the umami flavor. / Stop being so pretentious, Kyle. / Sorry.
jokes.setup: Cook-off tasters review Chris's burger
jokes.punchline: Kyle's attempt to be an informed food critic ('I love the umami flavor') is immediately and savagely shut down with 'Stop being so pretentious, Kyle' — someone eating a burger at a government cook-off is being called out for pretension
jokes.explanation: The 'umami' comment and its immediate smack-down is funny because it's the correct amount of clout-chasing for a City Hall burger cook-off. Kyle's 'Sorry' after being called pretentious is the perfect beaten button.

jokes.text: Here's mine. It's a hamburger, made out of meat, on a bun, with nothing. Add ketchup if you want. I couldn't care less.
jokes.setup: Ron presents his burger after Chris's elaborate presentation
jokes.punchline: Ron's burger is defined purely by what it ISN'T — no fancy ingredients, no presentation speech, just 'meat on a bun, with nothing.' The 'I couldn't care less' about the ketchup dismisses even that minimal condiment
jokes.explanation: The perfect comedic counterpoint to Chris's elaborate presentation. 'It's a hamburger, made out of meat, on a bun, with nothing' is Ron Swanson's entire food philosophy in one sentence. The structural contrast with Chris's preceding speech makes it funnier. 'Add ketchup if you want. I couldn't care less.' is the ideal button — he offers options but expresses total indifference to the choice. This justifies 8+ for its exceptional character integration (9.5), economy (9.5), and structural placement as the anti-presentation to Chris's elaborate one. This is a quotable, culturally resonant Ron Swanson moment.

jokes.text: Ron, I am so disappointed. I thought that you and I were gonna have a real challenge. [Beat] Never mind. This is better.
jokes.setup: Chris tastes Ron's burger expecting it to be inferior
jokes.punchline: He starts to deliver a condescending speech, pauses mid-sentence, and then abruptly reverses — 'Never mind. This is better.' — suggesting Ron's plain burger defeated his elaborate one
jokes.explanation: The misdirection is beautifully clean. Chris begins the condescending speech we expect from him, then the taste interrupts his own narrative. 'Never mind. This is better.' is a brilliant four-word defeat — the person who spent years perfecting a turkey burger recipe is undone in real time. The mid-sentence reversal is the structural key. Justifies 8+ for structure and economy.

jokes.text: Turkey can never beat cow, Chris. Sorry.
jokes.setup: The cook-off has been decided; Ron won
jokes.punchline: Ron delivers this as if consoling Chris on a loss that was always going to happen — 'Sorry' is performatively sympathetic but he's not sorry at all
jokes.explanation: The condescending 'Sorry' as a button on Ron's victory is excellent. He frames his win as an immutable law of nature ('turkey can never beat cow') rather than a personal achievement, which is very Ron. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Well, I don't understand. I've tinkered with this recipe for years. Granted, it's been a long time since I've had a hamburger. [Chris tastes Ron's burger properly for the first time]
jokes.setup: Chris is confused about how his elaborate recipe lost to a plain hamburger
jokes.punchline: The revelation that Chris hasn't eaten a hamburger in years means he has no reference point — he's been optimizing a recipe against a competitor he can't actually remember, making his years of 'tinkering' meaningless
jokes.explanation: 'Granted, it's been a long time since I've had a hamburger.' This retroactively reframes the entire cook-off. Chris spent years perfecting a turkey burger to beat a burger he hasn't eaten in years and thus can't accurately replicate in memory. The revelation collapses his whole enterprise. This justifies 8+ because it's a retroactive misdirection that recontextualizes the cook-off premise.

jokes.text: [Chris bites Ron's burger and has a revelation face — this is the visual payoff moment]
jokes.setup: Chris is about to accept defeat; instead he tries the burger and has an epiphany
jokes.punchline: The visual of Chris — the health food zealot — experiencing what appears to be a religious experience eating a plain hamburger validates everything Ron believes about food
jokes.explanation: The visual of a health nut having a profound experience eating the simplest possible hamburger is a strong payoff beat for the whole cook-off arc. The audience gets to see Chris's food ideology crumble in real time.

jokes.text: The commissary will continue to serve horrifying, artery-clogging hamburgers.
jokes.setup: Chris concedes the cook-off to Ron
jokes.punchline: His concession announcement uses his own health-framing language ('horrifying, artery-clogging') to describe the thing he has now agreed to allow — he's giving in while maintaining his objection
jokes.explanation: Chris announcing the return of burgers with his own negative descriptors intact is perfect — he loses the cook-off but refuses to lose his worldview. 'Horrifying, artery-clogging hamburgers' as the official commissary description is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Man. We spent, like, 50 hours working on those burgers. / I know. / Hard work never pays off. / Cooking is dumb.
jokes.setup: The cook-off is over; Andy and Chris process the defeat
jokes.punchline: Andy draws the lesson 'Hard work never pays off. Cooking is dumb.' — a sweeping negative conclusion from a specific event, delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Andy's philosophical conclusion — 'Hard work never pays off. Cooking is dumb.' — is perfect Andy Dwyer. He takes a specific disappointment and elevates it to universal law, and the laws are wrong in the funniest possible way. High character integration and strong economy.

jokes.text: I swear on this dead crow that I will never cook for you.
jokes.setup: Andy vows to Chris after the cook-off loss
